## How to use these notes

Slides 1-8 are the main talk. Slide 9 gives references; slides 10 onward are backups for questions. The English blocks below are the spoken script; the supplementary decision notes are for preparation, not extra speech to read aloud. Read the script with the actual slides and confirm a pace comfortable for each speaker.

Suggested allocation: Speaker 1, slides 1-2; Speaker 2, slides 3-4; Speaker 3, slides 5-6; Speaker 4, slides 7-8. This is a proposed allocation for four people, not evidence of actual contribution or agreement. Confirm names within the group. Timing is estimated from the current spoken word count; rehearse at a comfortable pace. The main paragraphs include the main transitions. Separate handover alternatives are preparation notes, not extra paragraphs to add to the timed talk. No human rehearsal is claimed.

We used the data handling, plots, bootstrap ideas and fairness criteria from our course. For unfamiliar modelling and evaluation methods, we asked ChatGPT for explanations and checked documentation, then rewrote and ran the main R analysis. ChatGPT also assisted initial code and text drafts, source checks and slide formatting. We checked the outputs and take responsibility for the final work.

Quiz 7 recommended Data to Viz, which prompted the figure review described below. The listed Data to Viz pages were actually consulted for this revision. These are optional design choices, not extra marking requirements. The review paragraphs are for preparation and questions; the eight spoken blocks remain the main script.

## Slide 1: the question

::: {.spoken data-slide="1" data-speaker="Speaker 1"}
Our question is whether information known at enrolment can identify later recorded dropout, and who the same warning rule misses. We are interested in student support. We first define the outcome, then evaluate overall prediction, and finally check how errors differ between groups. We start with the label, because it determines what a warning can mean.
:::

Our primary question concerns prediction, followed by whether the same rule is equally reliable across groups. We frame the warning around possible student support, not a judgement about an individual.

Transition: Before building a warning, we needed to understand what the recorded outcome actually meant.

## Slide 2: the outcome definition

::: {.spoken data-slide="2" data-speaker="Speaker 1"}
We used `r num(r$audit$rows)` records from one Portuguese institution. We checked the original paper because dropout can mean different things. Here it includes changing course or institution, so it does not always mean leaving higher education. The outcomes were recorded at the normal end of the course, usually three years. We retained students still enrolled. In our binary analysis they have no recorded dropout at that point; they are not assumed to have graduated. These choices define what our predictions can mean.
:::

The recorded label includes changing course or institution, rather than only leaving higher education. The endpoint is the normal course duration, usually three years and four for Nursing. Enrolled means no recorded dropout at that endpoint; it does not mean graduated or never dropping out later.

We retained the three original outcome labels and defined the binary endpoint explicitly. Removing Enrolled records would change the study population and the meaning of the question.

Transition: With that definition in place, we looked at what was already known at enrolment.

**Our figure-review explanation (not additional speech):** We wanted the audience to see all three recorded outcomes, including students still enrolled. After checking the [axis advice](https://www.data-to-viz.com/caveat/cut_y_axis.html), we kept the existing bars: they already started at zero and gave both counts and percentages. We did not change a chart that already supported this comparison. Its colours distinguish categories; their order does not rank students.

::: {.decision-note-en}
Our reasoning: We kept Enrolled because our question concerns recorded dropout at the stated endpoint. Removing those students would change the population. We therefore call them no recorded dropout at that point, without claiming they graduated.
:::


## Slide 3: what the entry profiles show

::: {.spoken data-slide="3" data-speaker="Speaker 2"}
These plots use training records only. The dropout group had a higher median age, but ages and admission grades still overlapped. Quiz 7 pointed us to Data to Viz. Its boxplot advice reminded us to show group sizes, so we added the counts below each outcome. We kept the boxes to compare typical values and spread. These observed patterns are associations, not causes.
:::

These are training-data boxplots. The distributions overlap even where their centres differ. The plots describe associations and cannot establish causes or an inevitable individual outcome.

We show spread and overlap alongside typical values. A few means alone could suggest a cleaner separation than the records support.

**Our figure-review explanation (not additional speech):** We wanted a quick comparison of typical values and spread. Quiz 7 recommended Data to Viz, which led us to review these figures. The [boxplot page](https://www.data-to-viz.com/caveat/boxplot.html) pointed out that boxes can hide group sizes and distribution shapes. We kept boxplots for this limited comparison and added the training counts: Graduate 1,324, Enrolled 476 and Dropout 852. Equal-width boxes should not suggest equal numbers of students. We did not add thousands of raw dots to the main slide, and we do not claim the boxes reveal every distribution feature. The two panels use different, explicitly labelled units; we compare outcomes within each panel.

Transition: We then needed a small model and a fair test of its predictions.

## Slide 4: inputs and evaluation design

::: {.spoken data-slide="4" data-speaker="Speaker 2"}
We used age, admission grade and course, excluding later semester results and financial fields with unclear timing. We used course tools for summaries and plots. Logistic regression and validation were new to us, so we asked ChatGPT for explanations, checked R documentation, then rewrote and checked the main analysis. Training records fit the model. Validation records chose the threshold. Test records evaluated the frozen rule. Recorded gender was reserved for the main audit. A probability still needs a threshold before it becomes a warning.
:::

Our primary inputs are age at enrolment, admission grade and course. Logistic regression produces estimated probabilities. Course is categorical; age and grade enter linearly on the log-odds scale, with additive course effects and no interactions. These are simplifying assumptions.

In the training records, attendance regime was determined by course. We therefore retain course without the redundant attendance term. This decision uses training data, rather than the later validation or test scores.

The partitions contain `r num(r$configuration$training_n)` training, `r num(r$configuration$validation_n)` validation and `r num(r$configuration$test_n)` test records. Validation chooses the threshold; it is not subsequently added back into the fitted model.

Transition: The next choice was how much estimated risk should trigger a warning.

::: {.decision-note-en}
Our reasoning: We want an enrolment warning, so a useful predictor must be known at enrolment. Later grades may predict well but answer a different question. We therefore keep a small set of defensible inputs and leave timing-uncertain fields out.
:::


## Slide 5: the warning threshold

::: {.spoken data-slide="5" data-speaker="Speaker 3"}
We wanted to find at least seventy per cent of dropout records in validation data while limiting false warnings. This illustrative target selected a common threshold of 0.31. It found 200 of 284 validation dropouts, about seventy per cent. We then froze the rule. The next slide checks test sensitivity and precision, and the cost in false warnings.
:::

The model produces a probability and the threshold converts it into a warning decision. A lower threshold generally finds more recorded dropouts while producing more false warnings. We select among validation thresholds attaining the illustrative 70% sensitivity target, maximising specificity; test outcomes do not choose the threshold.

The 70% target makes a trade-off explicit. It was not provided as university policy, and we do not have actual support-capacity data with which to establish an optimal operational policy.

**Our figure-review explanation (not additional speech):** We wanted to show how three rates change as the numerical threshold moves. The [axis discussion](https://www.data-to-viz.com/caveat/cut_y_axis.html) helped us distinguish this purpose from comparing bar lengths. We kept the lines and the full 0-100% scale. The [colour caveats](https://www.data-to-viz.com/caveats.html) also reminded us to consider readers who cannot distinguish our colours. We gave the three curves different line patterns, so colour is no longer the only way to follow them. These are observed validation rates, not confidence bands; the selected threshold is still 0.31.

Transition: We froze that choice and then checked what happened in the held-out test set.

::: {.decision-note-en}
Our reasoning: We use the seventy per cent validation target to make our trade-off explicit. It is our illustrative choice, not university policy. Once it selects a threshold, we keep that rule fixed so the test set can still provide a separate evaluation.
:::


## Slide 6: the actual test results

::: {.spoken data-slide="6" data-speaker="Speaker 3"}
Sensitivity tells us how many dropout records we find; precision tells us how many warnings match a dropout. Lowering the threshold found 107 more dropout records, but produced 177 more false warnings. Our chosen rule found 187 of 285 dropouts: about sixty-six per cent. Only 187 of its 409 warnings matched dropout: about forty-six per cent. Always giving no warning scores higher on accuracy, but finds no dropouts. That is why accuracy alone does not answer our question. We next ask who our rule misses.
:::

At threshold 0.50, the same 889 test records yield 80 true warnings and 45 false warnings; at 0.31, they yield 187 and 222. The change identifies 107 additional recorded dropouts with 177 additional false warnings. For the chosen rule, precision is `r pct(m$PPV)` and `r pct(m$WarningRate)` of records receive a warning.

The conditional bootstrap interval for sensitivity `r pct(m$Sensitivity)` is `r interval_pct(subset(r$overall_intervals,metric=="Sensitivity")$lower,subset(r$overall_intervals,metric=="Sensitivity")$upper)`. It is not a guarantee for future cohorts or students at another institution.

Finding more recorded dropouts can coincide with lower accuracy. We therefore report the gains and false-warning costs rather than treating accuracy as the sole objective.

Alternative transition (already included in the main script): An overall average cannot tell us who is missed. We next compare these errors across recorded-gender groups.

::: {.decision-note-en}
Our reasoning: We cannot judge this warning by accuracy alone. Always predicting no dropout already gives 67.9% accuracy, while finding none of the recorded dropouts. We therefore report who is found and how many warnings are false, with separate denominators.
:::


## Slide 7: whom the rule misses

::: {.spoken data-slide="7" data-speaker="Speaker 4"}
We focus first on missed dropouts, because a missed warning could mean a missed offer of support. The rule missed 64 of 144 female dropout records and 34 of 141 male records: forty-four versus twenty-four per cent. The gap was about twenty percentage points, with a conditional interval of roughly ten to thirty-one points. Male students had a higher false-warning rate. The other rows check who receives warnings and recorded outcomes within both prediction groups. These are independence, separation and sufficiency. Different recorded dropout rates complicate those comparisons; the gaps alone do not establish discrimination.
:::

Of 98 missed records, 64 were female and 34 male. The corresponding false-negative rates use actual dropout records as denominators: 64/144 and 34/141. The female-minus-male gap is about 20.3 percentage points, with a conditional interval of about 9.5 to 30.7 points.

How we applied the three fairness criteria:

- We compare warning rates across all records in each group for Independence.
- We compare false-positive and false-negative rates for Separation. Female records have the higher missed-dropout rate; male records have the higher false-warning rate.
- For binary Sufficiency, we compare actual outcomes within both warned and unwarned prediction strata. Checking precision alone would omit the second stratum.

Leaving gender out of the primary model does not establish fairness: course and other inputs may still be associated with gender. The groups have different recorded dropout proportions, so warning rates, error rates and predictive values answer different questions. This audit measures gaps; it does not separate their causes. We have not tested a policy of different thresholds by group.

**Our figure-review explanation (not additional speech):** We wanted to compare error rates, but a group's total is not the denominator of every rate. The [sample-size caveat](https://www.data-to-viz.com/caveats.html) prompted us to put the relevant n beside every point. For missed dropouts, those denominators are 144 female and 141 male dropout records, rather than all 575 and 314 students. We kept points with intervals because we are displaying binary rates and sampling uncertainty. The [error-bar page](https://www.data-to-viz.com/caveat/error_bar.html) stresses that bars can mean different things, so we explicitly identify ours as pointwise 95% percentile bootstrap intervals, conditional on the fixed model and threshold. They are not standard deviations or a guarantee about a future cohort. We also added circle and triangle markers. To compare the groups directly, we use the gap intervals in backup slide 12 rather than treating overlap of two separate intervals as a formal test.

Alternative transition (already included in the main script): These group differences lead us to the checks we would require before real use.

::: {.decision-note-en}
Our reasoning: We compare missed-dropout rates within actual dropouts, because the groups have different sizes. The relevant comparison is 64/144 against 34/141. We also keep false warnings and both prediction strata, so our fairness discussion covers more than one favourable statistic.
:::


## Slide 8: the conclusion and next step

::: {.spoken data-slide="8" data-speaker="Speaker 4"}
Our enrolment model found about two-thirds of recorded dropouts, with many false warnings and different error rates across groups. Before real use, we would check departure reasons, support capacity and performance on later cohorts at the intended institution. Any warning should lead to human review, with a way to correct records. We have not tested whether acting on warnings prevents dropout. That needs a separate evaluation of the support offered. Thank you.
:::

The results support further investigation of a possible warning signal, rather than immediate deployment. Real use would require checks of label meaning, support capacity, later cohorts and other institutions, together with human review and correction of records. Whether support actually reduces dropout requires a separate intervention study.

## Our learning and implementation process

We applied methods from our course: categorical factors, grouped summaries, joins, ggplot layers, faceting, bootstrap ideas and the three fairness criteria. We used these tools to understand the data and report comparisons with clear denominators.

Logistic regression, held-out evaluation, threshold selection, AUC and Brier score needed further learning. We asked ChatGPT what each method measures and why it fits our question, checked the documentation, then rewrote and ran the main R analysis. We checked the outputs against the raw records and saved predictions. The bootstrap idea came from class; applying it to several group rates needed extra implementation guidance.

Our statistical interpretation remains our responsibility. ChatGPT also helped with initial code and text drafts, source checks and slide formatting. We need to explain the inputs, assumptions and denominators, as well as show that the code runs.

## Figure-review notes for backup slides

**Slide 12 — keep the gap intervals.** We wanted a direct comparison of two groups, so we retained the male-minus-female gap plot and its zero reference line. Following the [error-bar advice](https://www.data-to-viz.com/caveat/error_bar.html), we describe the exact interval construction. These are pointwise intervals for five separate metrics, not simultaneous certification that a rule is fair.

**Slide 13 — keep the bootstrap histogram.** We retained its original 35 bins and percentile lines. The numerical limits come from all 5,000 stored bootstrap estimates, not from visually choosing histogram bins. We did not run or claim an experiment comparing bin widths during this review.

**Slide 14 — distinguish the groups without colour alone.** We wanted to inspect probabilities separately from binary warnings. Following the [colour caveats](https://www.data-to-viz.com/caveats.html), we added the same female circle and male triangle used on slide 7. Point size still encodes n. We now explicitly state that no intervals are displayed; the sparse-bin omission and descriptive interpretation remain unchanged. We do not infer precise calibration from points near the diagonal.

**Slide 18 — make the order deliberate.** We wanted to compare course composition. After reading [Why you should order your data](https://www.data-to-viz.com/caveat/order_data.html), we replaced alphabetical order with descending pooled training counts for the six named courses. We left Other courses last because it combines the remaining courses. The legend now states the female and male training totals, 1,720 and 932. We retained zero-based horizontal bars, consistent with the [axis advice](https://www.data-to-viz.com/caveat/cut_y_axis.html). The bar lengths still show shares within each group, not pooled counts. We have made the reading order clearer without changing the model or claiming this explains the error gap.

## First-person explanations you can use selectively

These are alternatives to use when asked, not extra paragraphs to add to every slide. Review them against your own understanding.

| Decision reflected in the actual work | English explanation |
| --- | --- |
| Fix the prediction time | We first needed to decide what early meant. We chose enrolment, so later semester results could not enter our model. |
| Check the measured outcome | We checked the original paper before treating the word dropout as a simple measure of leaving university. |
| Retain Enrolled | We kept students who were still enrolled and described their status honestly, rather than treating them as graduates. |
| Exclude financial timing uncertainty | We could not establish when each financial status was recorded, so we left those fields out of the enrolment model. |
| Avoid redundant inputs | Our training cross-tabulation showed that course already determined attendance regime in this dataset. |
| Evaluate the actual support trade-off | We looked at false warnings as well as missed records, because both affect the resources and people involved. |
| Avoid claiming fairness from omission | We left recorded gender out of the primary predictors, then checked the errors by gender instead of assuming the omission solved the problem. |

## Questions to practise

### Does higher accuracy mean a better warning rule?

Not for this purpose on its own. Always giving no warning is correct for 604 of 889 records (67.9%), but finds none of the 285 recorded dropouts. The chosen rule is correct for 569 records (64.0%), finds 187 dropouts and produces 222 false warnings. Whether that trade-off is acceptable depends on support capacity and the consequences of each error; these data do not establish an optimal policy.

### What do the three fairness criteria ask here?

Independence asks whether students in each recorded-gender group receive warnings at the same rate: 218/575 female records (37.9%) versus 191/314 male records (60.8%). Separation checks errors conditional on the actual label: false-warning rates are 138/431 (32.0%) and 84/173 (48.6%); missed-dropout rates are 64/144 (44.4%) and 34/141 (24.1%). Binary Sufficiency checks outcomes within both prediction groups: dropout among warned records is 80/218 (36.7%) versus 107/191 (56.0%); dropout among unwarned records is 64/357 (17.9%) versus 34/123 (27.6%). These are conditional comparisons, not interchangeable measures or a causal verdict.

### Does a 20-point gap prove discrimination?

No. The female-minus-male missed-dropout gap is about 20.3 percentage points in this held-out sample. Its interval conditions on the fitted model and threshold. It does not include all model-development uncertainty, account for unavailable cohort structure, or explain why the groups differ. The pattern warrants investigation before any use; it does not establish a causal explanation or identify who needs support.

### Which test counts support sensitivity and precision?

We found 187 of the 285 recorded dropouts, giving sensitivity of 65.6%. We issued 409 warnings; 187 matched a dropout record, giving precision of 45.7%. The other 222 warnings were false positives relative to the recorded endpoint. We missed 98 dropout records and correctly left 382 other records unflagged. We use these counts to explain the denominators rather than treating every percentage as accuracy.

### Why use this dataset and this question?

The brief lists UCI as a source for alternative datasets. This release has an accessible source, numerical and categorical variables, and enough student records for a manageable project. Our question connects prediction to a concrete support concern. Dataset feasibility still needs the lecturer/course organiser's confirmation.

### What exactly does a positive outcome mean?

Recorded Dropout at the source's normal course endpoint. The paper includes course and institution changes. It does not necessarily mean abandoning all higher education, and it is not a direct observation of who needs support.

### Why retain students who are still enrolled?

The primary endpoint is recorded dropout by that point. Enrolled students have not been recorded as Dropout then, though they may leave later. The separate resolved-outcome check makes the consequences of excluding them visible; it cannot silently replace the primary population.

### Why not use the very predictive second-semester grades?

They were not available at the chosen prediction time. They could support a different, later-stage question, but would not test an enrolment warning.

### Why logistic regression, and is it in the supplied slides?

We had not used logistic regression in the supplied course material. We used AI explanations and official R documentation to learn how it models a binary outcome and returns probabilities, then reimplemented and checked the analysis. We treated course as categorical. We also learned that our age and grade terms are linear on the log-odds scale, with no interactions; these are assumptions we need to explain.

### Why only three predictors?

They have a defensible enrolment interpretation and keep the model explainable. We chose scope over a broad feature search. This does not prove other entry variables are irrelevant or that this model is optimal.

### Why three partitions?

We needed extra explanation of held-out evaluation. We learned to give each partition a different job: training fits coefficients, validation chooses the rule, and test estimates performance after both are fixed. We implemented this split in R and kept validation records out of the final fit. We did not use test results to choose the threshold.

### Why seventy per cent?

We chose seventy per cent as an illustrative validation sensitivity goal. We learned how a threshold trades missed records against false warnings, then implemented a rule that maximised specificity among the eligible validation thresholds. We do not present our target as university policy or an objectively optimal choice. Real use would require consultation about benefits, costs and capacity.

### What does AUC tell us?

We learned that AUC measures ranking rather than threshold-based accuracy. Our primary test AUC is `r num(m$AUC,3)`, with a conditional bootstrap interval of `r num(subset(r$overall_intervals,metric=="AUC")$lower,3)` to `r num(subset(r$overall_intervals,metric=="AUC")$upper,3)`. We interpret it as how often a randomly selected dropout record receives a higher score than a non-dropout record, counting ties halfway. We do not treat this as proof of calibration or usefulness at a particular threshold.

### What does Brier score tell us?

We learned to evaluate the probabilities as well as the binary warnings. We used Brier score, the mean squared difference between predicted probability and the zero/one outcome; lower is better on comparable records. Our primary test value is `r num(m$Brier,3)`, versus `r num(r$metrics$Brier[1],3)` for the training-prevalence baseline.

### Why is female FNR higher even though gender was not an input?

Omitting a recorded attribute does not remove differences carried by other inputs, course composition or underlying outcome patterns. This descriptive audit identifies a difference. It does not isolate its cause or prove intentional discrimination.

### Did adding gender solve the difference?

No. In this pre-specified comparison at the same threshold, AUC changed only slightly and the missed-dropout pattern became more unequal. That is why a small aggregate improvement cannot by itself determine a fair support rule. Both sets of results remain visible in the backup.

### Can all three fairness criteria hold?

They condition on different denominators and may conflict when groups have different outcome rates and predictions are imperfect. We do not require all three to hold or make an unconditional impossibility claim. Which error matters depends on the use and the people affected.

### What uncertainty does the bootstrap cover?

It resamples held-out student records within each recorded-gender group, with the fitted model and threshold held fixed. It describes variation in this conditional evaluation. It does not account for refitting the model, cohort clustering, transport to another institution or the effect of offering support. The intervals are pointwise, not simultaneous fairness certification.

### Is this a future-cohort test?

No. The release has no cohort/year field, so our random hold-out mixes historical cohorts. Prospective or chronological validation is an important missing step.

### What is still needed from the group?

Review the data definitions and code, obtain the required topic-feasibility confirmation, agree the speakers, practise aloud, attend check-ins, set up actual repository collaboration and complete the separately required report, peer evaluation and submissions. None is claimed completed by the slide files.

### What assistance was used?

We asked ChatGPT to explain unfamiliar methods and used its help with initial code and text drafts, source checks and slide formatting. We then rewrote and ran the main R analysis and checked the outputs. R generated the statistical results; we are responsible for our final interpretation.
